Latin Music's Global Moment: Bad Bunny, Karol G, Peso Pluma and the Business of Reggaeton and Regional Mexican

Curated & written by Rohan Verma

If you want proof that Spanish-language music has gone fully global, look at the numbers. Bad Bunny topped Pollstar's worldwide mid-year touring chart in 2026 with $225.1 million in ticket sales, a Latin-influenced song sits in the Hot 100 top ten, and Latin America accounts for almost a quarter of Spotify's paying subscribers. This is no longer a niche story.

Bad Bunny's Touring Dominance

Bad Bunny's mid-year figures were remarkable. Pollstar reported a gross of $225.1 million from 27 shows and around 1.4 million tickets, at an average price of about $150. In the separate ranking by average gross per city, he placed second in July with about $7.9 million per city, an average attendance near 57,900 and an average ticket price of $136.50. Those figures put him ahead of most rock and pop acts and reflect arena and stadium-size demand in market after market.

What is striking is that his success has not required him to compromise. His audience follows him into Spanish-language songs, and the pricing is relatively modest compared with some other major tours, which helps explain the volume.

Karol G and the Hot 100

On the singles side, Karol G's "Bby Wow," featuring Judeline and Rusowsky, holds No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 dated October 17, with a peak of No. 6 and nine weeks on the chart. Its presence among the biggest songs in the United States shows that listeners are no longer treating Spanish-language pop as a separate category. The collaboration with Rusowsky and Judeline also points to how younger, more experimental Spanish-language artists are being brought in alongside established stars.

Regional Mexican and Beyond

The genre's strength is not limited to reggaeton. Peso Pluma appeared on Pollstar's global tours list in both July rankings, with an average gross of roughly $1.55 million to $1.6 million per city. Romeo Santos and Prince Royce, who bring bachata to arenas, also placed on the lists, as did Pitbull and Ricardo Arjona. Together, they show a market that includes tropical, regional Mexican, pop and singer-songwriter styles, each with its own loyal following.

Latin Artists on the World Stage

Latin names also featured prominently at this summer's World Cup. Shakira, the Colombian star, teamed with Burna Boy on "Dai Dai," the tournament's official song, which reached No. 1 on the Global 200. On the FIFA album, Brazilian singer Anitta joined Rema and Thai star Lisa on "Goals," a track that blends Afrobeats, K-pop and Latin pop. The pairing of Latin, African and Asian artists is a sign of how pop music increasingly forms across regions.

The Streaming Foundation

The growth in listening helps explain these results. According to figures reported alongside Spotify's second-quarter earnings, Latin America accounts for 24 percent of Premium subscribers, nearly matching North America at 25 percent. As more listeners in the region pay for streaming, Latin artists accumulate larger and more reliable audiences. The relationship is circular: strong streaming supports touring, and strong touring supports streaming.

BTS in Latin America

The region is also a key market for other global acts. The BTS world tour, according to its originally announced schedule, includes dates in Bogotá, Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires and São Paulo in October. That route is a reminder that fans in the region are among the most passionate in the world, willing to travel and spend heavily to see their favourite artists.

The Awards Dimension

The wider Grammy organisation includes the Latin Recording Academy, which runs a separate awards programme, but the Latin presence on mainstream lists shows how little the boundaries matter to listeners. Whether an artist ultimately wins a Latin award or a general award, the audience has already voted with streams and tickets.

What Comes Next

The next big questions are about sustainability and diversity. Will the success of a few superstars open doors for emerging artists from smaller countries and scenes? Will Spanish-language collaborations continue to appear on major global projects? The trend lines suggest yes, as long as audiences keep rewarding authenticity.

For GanaTube listeners, the lesson is that language is no longer a barrier. A song that moves you can come from anywhere, and the best way to explore is to follow the collaborations. Start with the artists named here, then look at who they work with, and you will find a web of connections that stretches across continents.
